title: Part III — PRODUCT: The Product Operating Model

know: The part answers four questions in order, one per chapter: Why do organizations that ship a great deal still fail their customers, and what should they aim at instead?; How does a product vision become a strategy that teams can act on?; What should a roadmap commit to, and how far ahead can it honestly look?; What may a product team decide for itself, and how does that fit with a vision set at the top?
can_do: Pick the chapter of this part that answers the question in front of them.

audience.who: Executives and individual contributors in product and tech who have read Parts I and II and are about to start Part III, or who arrive with one question about product work and want the chapter that answers it.
already_knows: How software teams work day to day, and what a roadmap and a feature request are.
Parts I and II in outline: the organization as a system with decision rights among its levers, and as a product whose changes are judged by outcomes (chapter 2).
does_not_know: Output and outcome as the book defines them for the product (chapter 9); glossed here.
Key customer outcome and key business outcome (chapter 9); glossed here.
The customer-journey vision and a strategy that works backward from it (chapter 10); glossed here.
Roadmap horizons and the balance of innovation, iteration and operation (chapter 11); glossed here.
Problem space and solution space, discovery, delivery and product operations (chapter 12); glossed here.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can name the four chapters' subjects in reading order.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only this page: what will each of the next four chapters tell you, in order?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Outcomes Over Output; Vision and Product Strategy; Roadmaps and Horizons; Discovery, Delivery and Empowered Teams.

thesis.question: How does an organization decide what to build so that its teams deliver outcomes and not output?
thesis.claim: An organization delivers outcomes when a customer-journey vision bounds the problems worth solving, strategy sequences them, the roadmap states outcomes over horizons no longer than it has evidence for, and teams own the solutions; vision set at the top and empowerment at the edge do not conflict once the boundary between problem space and solution space is explicit.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that customers and the market decide what gets built, so that product work is collecting requests and delivering them on time; and the opposite view that teams should discover everything bottom-up and a vision from the top only constrains them.
thesis.so_what: A leader stops approving feature lists and starts stating outcomes and their order, and a team stops asking what to build and starts answering for a result.
thesis.how_why: A request names a solution, and a list of solutions carries no reason to prefer one to another or to stop. An outcome with a vision behind it gives teams a reason to choose and leaders a way to judge, and it leaves the choice of solution with the people closest to the customer and the code.

supporting_claims.claim: Organizations that measure themselves by what they ship fail their customers in recognizable ways, and the remedy is to make a customer outcome and a business outcome the unit of progress.
A vision described as the customer's future journey, with a strategy that works backward from it, is what turns outcomes from a slogan into an order of work.
A roadmap should commit to outcomes over horizons that shrink in certainty, and balance innovation, iteration and operation deliberately.
Leaders own the problem space and its order; teams own the solution space; and discovery, delivery and product operations are the machinery that lets a team use that ownership.

role.contribution: Performs the part's opening: states the part thesis and the reading order.

additional_patterns.applies_to: four-steps and the chapter list in the closing: outcome, then vision and strategy, then roadmap, then who decides

flow.rationale: The page opens on a roadmap that was delivered and changed nothing, and on the question of what the roadmap was for. The first section says why a list of requests cannot answer that question; the second gives the four steps that replace the list, says why they come in that order, resolves the apparent conflict between direction from the top and decisions in teams, and places the steps in the book's two lenses; the chapter list closes the page. The reason stands before the four steps because each step supplies something the list lacks; put the steps first and outcome, vision, roadmap and decision rights arrive as product vocabulary with no problem behind it. The list comes last because a reader can choose a chapter only after seeing what each decides.

hook.content: Corvane shipped forty-one features in a year, every one promised to a customer by name, and its renewal rate fell.

bridge.from_reader_world: The reader's experience of a roadmap that was delivered in full and changed nothing.
bridge.to_topic: The question that experience raises and that the usual explanations (wrong features, late delivery, sales promising too much) skip: what the roadmap was for.

thesis_statement.text: Part III argues that an organization delivers outcomes when a vision of the customer's future journey bounds the problems worth solving, a strategy puts them in order, the roadmap states outcomes only as far ahead as it has evidence for, and teams own the solutions; and that direction from the top and decisions in teams do not conflict once the line between problem and solution is explicit.

promises.promise: Why a list of requests cannot steer an organization.

The four steps that replace the list, and why they come in that order; four chapters answer four questions in order: what to aim at, how a vision becomes a strategy, what a roadmap commits to, and what a team decides for itself.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In one year Corvane shipped forty-one features, each promised to a named customer, and its renewal rate fell.

evidence.what: Corvane (fictional): in one year between 2022 and 2024, while growing to 180 people, it shipped forty-one features, each promised to a named customer; its roadmap was a list of such promises with dates; the renewal rate fell. Customers pay per technician per month.
evidence.shows: A roadmap delivered in full while the customers it was written for left.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A roadmap that is delivered and changes nothing is usually explained by the choice of features or the speed of delivery, and the question that explains it is what the roadmap was for, which Corvane's list did not say.

evidence.what: Corvane's roadmap (fictional) gave each feature, the customer it was promised to and a date; nothing on it said what should be different for a customer once a feature shipped.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (the last clause is appended by this page)
evidence.shows: The list could be finished without anyone being able to say whether it had worked.

transition_in.carries_over: The forty-one features and the falling renewal rate.
transition_in.introduces: The reader's own version of that roadmap, and the question that explains it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Part III argues that an organization delivers outcomes when a vision bounds the problems, a strategy orders them, the roadmap states outcomes as far as its evidence reaches and teams own the solutions, and that direction from the top and decisions in teams do not conflict once the line between problem and solution is explicit; it makes the argument in four chapters that answer four questions in order.

transition_in.carries_over: The question of what a roadmap is for.

sections.heading: Why a List of Requests Cannot Steer
sections.controlling_idea: A request names a solution, and a list of solutions carries no reason to prefer one item to another or to stop; an outcome with a vision behind it supplies that reason and leaves the choice of solution with the people closest to the customer and the code.

advances_thesis.how: States the reasoning from which the part derives its four steps.

transition_in.carries_over: The part's claim as stated in the lead.
transition_in.introduces: The reasoning that produces it: what a list of requests lacks.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Output is what an organization ships and an outcome is a change the customer can observe; a request names a solution, so a list of requests is a list of outputs with no reason in it to prefer one item to another or to stop.

evidence.what: A request names a solution; a list of solutions carries no reason to prefer one to another or to stop.
evidence.shows: Why a list of requests can be delivered in full and decide nothing.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An outcome with a vision behind it, a vision being a description of the customer's future experience, gives teams a reason to choose and leaders a way to judge, and it leaves the choice of solution with the people closest to the customer and the code.

evidence.what: An outcome with a vision behind it gives teams a reason to choose and leaders a way to judge, and leaves the solution with those closest to the customer and the code.
evidence.shows: What replaces the list has to state a result and a direction, and need not state the solution.

transition_in.carries_over: A list with no reason to prefer or to stop.
transition_in.introduces: What supplies the reason: an outcome with a vision behind it.

sections.heading: Four Steps from Outcome to Decision
sections.controlling_idea: Four steps replace the list (an outcome as the unit of progress, a vision and a strategy that order the outcomes, a roadmap that lays them out in time, and a stated division of decisions between leaders and teams), and each step needs the one before it.

advances_thesis.how: One list item per supporting claim, then the order, then the resolution of the thesis's apparent conflict, then the book's two lenses.

flow.rationale: Outcomes come first because vision and strategy are defined in terms of them; the roadmap follows because it is the strategy laid out in time; the division of decisions comes last because it needs all three to say who decides what. The paragraph on the order follows the list directly because it explains the list's sequence while the list is in front of the reader; the paragraph on the conflict follows because the conflict belongs to the last step and can be resolved only once that step has named the two spaces; the paragraph on the two lenses closes the section because it reads all four steps, and the resolution just given, as instances of the book's two disciplines. Put the division of decisions first and teams are handed decisions with no outcome to decide for.

transition_in.carries_over: An outcome with a vision behind it as what a list lacks.
transition_in.introduces: The four steps that supply it, one per chapter.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Four steps replace the list: a customer outcome and a business outcome as the unit of progress; a vision of the customer's future journey with a strategy that works backward from it; a roadmap that commits to outcomes over horizons of shrinking certainty and balances innovation, iteration and operation; and a division of decisions in which leaders own the problem space and its order while teams own the solution space.

advances_thesis.how: Names the four steps with their terms glossed, one per supporting claim.

evidence.what: Key customer outcome and key business outcome, the customer journey vision, product strategy working backward from it, and the balanced roadmap of innovation, iteration and operation, as defined in Build What Matters (Foster and Nerlikar, 2020).
evidence.source: Build What Matters; author's notes under _input/bookshelf/docs/notes/; journal-spec.json entries of chapters 9 to 12
evidence.shows: The terms are a named source's model, which chapters 9 to 11 present and test.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The four steps come in prerequisite order: outcomes first because a vision and a strategy are stated in terms of them, the roadmap third because it is the strategy laid out in time, and the division of decisions last because a team handed the choice of solution before any outcome is stated has nothing to decide for.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the four supporting claims as steps that depend on each other.

evidence.what: Vision and strategy are defined in terms of outcomes; the roadmap is the strategy laid out in time; the division of decisions needs all three; a division made first hands teams decisions with no outcome to decide for.
evidence.shows: Why the chapters are read in this order.

transition_in.introduces: The one direction in which they depend on each other.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Direction set at the top and decisions made in teams, the conflict the lead said the part resolves, do not conflict once the line between the problem space and the solution space is explicit, which answers both the view that product work is collecting requests and the view that any direction from the top constrains teams.

advances_thesis.how: States the second half of the part thesis against the two views that dispute it.

evidence.what: The vision bounds the problem space and leaves the solution space open; each level decides where it has the information.

transition_in.carries_over: The division of decisions as the last step.
transition_in.introduces: The conflict that step is usually thought to contain, and why it does not.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The four steps carry the book's two lenses: they are the product thinking that chapter 2 applied to the organization, shown here on the product built for customers, and the fourth step is the decision-right lever of system design applied to product work.

advances_thesis.how: Places the part's steps, and the division of decisions in particular, in the book's two disciplines.

evidence.what: Chapter 2 took outcome, discovery and roadmap from product work and applied them to the organization; the division of decisions between leaders and teams is the decision-right lever of chapter 1 applied to product work.

conclusion.heading: Chapters in this part
conclusion.synthesis: The four chapters put four things in the place of one list, and each answers something the list could not: what to aim at, in which order, by when and with how much certainty, and who chooses the solution.
conclusion.so_what: A leader stops approving feature lists and starts stating outcomes and their order, and a team stops asking what to build and starts answering for a result.

callback.to: Corvane's forty-one features and its roadmap of promises from the opening (p01, p02).
callback.how: The closing reads the list against the four questions: it said what would ship, for whom and when, and answered none of the four.

takeaway.content: Read the chapters in order; with one question about product work in hand, open the chapter that answers it.

hand_off.carries_over: The part's claim that an organization should deliver outcomes and not output.
hand_off.introduces: What output-driven organizations look like, and what an outcome is.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each of the four chapters answers one question, in this order: what to aim at instead of output, how a vision becomes a strategy, what a roadmap commits to, and what a team decides for itself.

The four chapters put four answers in the place of one list, none of which Corvane's list of promises gave; a leader who has them stops approving feature lists and states outcomes and their order, and the first chapter starts with what output-driven organizations look like and what an outcome is.

transition_in.introduces: What they add up to for Corvane's list and for the reader, and the first chapter.
